items.subject: ASML Is Building a Hybrid Bonding Tool!
items.body:
View this post on the web at https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/asml-is-building-a-hybrid-bonding

ASML has not announced anything yet, but its patent filings, a news report [ https://substack.com/redirect/98cb15a0-657a-4a29-b8b4-c9aad8b398c1?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ] and its own roadmap all suggest so. We believe it will start with a die-to-wafer (D2W) hybrid bonding (HB) tool. This is harder to build than wafer-to-wafer but is where ASML could gain an edge. We see the move as a natural extension of ASML’s vertical integration, and one that should strengthen its customer ties.
In this article we unpack the tool’s design end to end, starting with patent filings. What makes it unique is that it runs on a track. That changes how the tool and the dies move: each die rides its own holder past the process stations, and the tools get closer at each station to process the dies. The track’s independent shuttles also lift station utilization, save on duplicate tooling, and enable heterogeneous integration.
We believe ASML could gain an edge in alignment accuracy and particle control for Hybrid Bonding. These are the two factors that set bonding yield. And ASML has expertise in solving the same problems in lithography.
Despite the advantages, ASML still needs to solve challenges around feed-forward metrology, the die-to-wafer contact, the modification of the non-bonding tools so they can process dies on the track, and keeping the whole loop clean.
We expect advanced logic, where D2W already runs in volume, to adopt ASML’s D2W HB tool first. This is bad news for Besi. Logic accounts for most of Besi’s HB business today concentrated at TSMC and Intel. ASML has been working with both for more than two decades and just announced a joint photomask initiative in September. We won’t be surprised to see a similar move in the back end process. Besi’s HBM prospects are also weakening. Korean challengers are catching up, in addition to an HBM adoption that we expect [ https://substack.com/redirect/5cac5dd0-8a4a-4dd7-879f-5a40d13d5c72?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ] to slip to 2029 or beyond.
ASML is Building a Hybrid Bonder
We did a deep dive on hybrid bonding [ https://substack.com/redirect/8185c97a-3faa-4e28-87e3-7d4d2df8bd66?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ] in 2024, and we still see it as the most transformative innovation in semiconductor manufacturing since EUV. Wafer-to-wafer (W2W) hybrid bonding (HB) is already in volume in image sensors and 3D NAND, and DRAM makers will be next. Die-to-wafer (D2W) HB is moving slower, because the industry still lacks mature tools that combine satisfying alignment accuracy and throughput (our check indicates upper bound in current applications is only one wafer per hour), which keeps cost per die high. Today D2W runs in volume only in logic: AMD has shipped hybrid-bonded V-Cache since 2022, and TSMC’s SoIC bonds at about 6um pitch today and targets 4.5um around 2029. The market expected HBM to become the big D2W volume driver from 2028. However, our view is different: we believe HBM will not adopt D2W HB before 2029 [ https://substack.com/redirect/5cac5dd0-8a4a-4dd7-879f-5a40d13d5c72?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ], if at all.
Besi has led D2W and is the only supplier with tools in volume production. Everyone else is still trying to get a first tool qualified. But we believe the situation will soon change, because ASML is building a D2W hybrid bonding tool. Management hasn’t announced anything yet. But the company filed 27 bonding patent families between December 2022 and November 2024, most of them D2W, and the true count is likely higher because filings made after November 2024 are not yet public. The Elec [ https://substack.com/redirect/98cb15a0-657a-4a29-b8b4-c9aad8b398c1?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ] also reported in March that ASML had started the architecture design of a hybrid bonder with Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG.
In the anchor filing (WO2025201788A1 [ https://substack.com/redirect/732ef78d-f92b-420a-b6d0-88af600d522d?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ]), ASML drew how its bonding flow works. Interestingly, the system looks nothing like a traditional D2W bonder (see Advanced Packaging Part 5 [ https://substack.com/redirect/8185c97a-3faa-4e28-87e3-7d4d2df8bd66?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ] for how those work). Instead of a bond head picking each die off a diced wafer and placing it, ASML moves single dies on independent holders around a track (Fig 1). Each die passes inspection, cleaning, plasma activation and metrology (topography, leveling and alignment) stations before it reaches the bonding station where the chuck lifts the bottom wafer up to meet the die. We unpack the design in the sections below.
Fig 1: ASML’s track-based D2W bonder, SA annotated and simplified
ASML could be building a W2W hybrid bonding tool as well. According to a patent analysis by Inha University [ https://substack.com/redirect/eb7cc2e7-b7df-4bd4-ad08-dcc7a80bb077?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ], ASML is likely building W2W HB equipment on its TWINSCAN platform, leaning on its wafer overlay accuracy. We focus on the D2W machine in this note, because it is the harder tool to build and the one where ASML could gain a real edge.
…as Part of its Vertical Integration Initiative
We believe this is a continuation of ASML’s effort to integrate vertically and tighten customer relationships. ASML bought Cymer for its light source in 2013, HMI for e-beam inspection in 2016 and Berliner Glas for optics modules in 2020. It shipped [ https://substack.com/redirect/0f58e2df-2211-45ab-bbcb-cd283e5cfee1?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ] its first back-end product, the XT:260 i-line packaging scanner, in 3Q25. And most recently, ASML announced joint initiatives with TSMC [ https://substack.com/redirect/093f4013-8bd0-435a-8dfb-8a7d8c65d906?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ], Intel Foundry [ https://substack.com/redirect/d5c90592-2f5b-4d7a-90ff-94d17e031258?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ] and Samsung [ https://substack.com/redirect/3f8311a5-9ec9-43c6-baa9-52e8a31116d9?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ] to move the industry from 6-inch to 12-inch photomasks for High NA EUV.
Building a bonder would be a natural next step. In fact, ASML’s own roadmap already puts bonding inside the front-end flow. Its 2024 Investor Day listed W2W and D2W hybrid bonding for NAND, DRAM and logic (Fig 2). And a July 2024 filing [ https://substack.com/redirect/ad19bd9e-cc4a-4054-908f-c744f6b75970?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ] shows how the bonder and the scanner would work together by sharing die position data. Today a scanner printing on a bonded wafer must pre-align and coarse-align every die before it can expose. In ASML’s design the bonder already knows where it put each die and hands that map (a “coordinate system” in the filing) to the scanner, which checks a few marks and exposes. Customers get faster lithography on bonded wafers, and ASML gets to sell the bonder and the scanner as a pair.
Fig 2: ASML’s map of front-end 3D integration
We expect advanced logic to be the first adopter. Logic is where D2W HB already runs in volume, and where the alignment requirement keeps tightening. TSMC calls overlay “always the biggest challenge” for SoIC. As its HB pitch moves from 6um to 4.5um by 2029, the placement accuracy requirement will tighten further. ASML is strong in alignment, as we will elaborate below, so an edge here should help it win logic customers first. Advanced logic dies are also among the most expensive c

items.subject: The Age of Programmable Biology
items.body:
View this post on the web at https://metatrends.substack.com/p/the-age-of-programmable-biology

TLDR: The convergence of Superintelligence (SI) and synthetic biology is turning biology into an engineering discipline. Colossal Biosciences built an end-to-end platform for that work and proved it in public when it revived the dire wolf, and designed the woolly mouse. Today I’m proud to announcing NeoGenesis Capital [ https://substack.com/redirect/9fd800c2-7b58-466b-99c2-7ceb5dacb5a0?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ], in partnership with Yianni Psaltis, PhD, investing in Colossal and the myriad of future companies built on its platform.
For the past two decades, genetic engineering was slow, narrow and expensive. You could edit a gene, maybe a few. Designing an organism was science fiction. The distance between reading life and writing it was the defining limit of the field, and most people assumed it would stay that way for decades.
It didn’t.
The cost of sequencing a human genome has fallen from about $100 million in 2001 to roughly $200 today. That’s a 500,000-fold drop, which makes Moore’s Law look slow. AI can now model what a change to a genome will do before anyone touches a cell. Multiplex editing can write dozens of those changes at once. Stack those curves and you get something new: the ability to design living products in silico… how they grow, how they function, and how they look, and then making them real.
And the biggest players in science see it coming. Last week the Chan Zuckerberg Biohub, the Department of Energy, the NIH, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs and Meta committed $1.8 billion to generate the data for an AI “virtual cell.”
“We spent the last half century learning to read life. The next decade is about designing it, writing it and producing it.”
WHY I WROTE ONE OF THE FIRST CHECK
In 2021, I was among the first investors in Colossal Biosciences, the company Ben Lamm and George Church founded to bring back the woolly mammoth. (Yes, everyone asks about Jurassic Park. Ben’s answer: there’s no viable dinosaur DNA left, so relax.)
I said yes because of the two of them. George is as close as we have to the father of synthetic biology. Ben is one of the best builders I know; he had started and sold five companies before Colossal. I’ve spent 30 years running XPRIZE, and I have never once seen a team regret aiming too high. A team that sets out to resurrect a species is aiming about as high as you can.
I expected a Moonshot. What I didn’t expect was that the platform underneath the Moonshot would matter more than the animal.
The world saw the headlines: the woolly mouse in March 2025 (the fluffiest proof of concept in scientific history), then Romulus, Remus and Khaleesi, the first dire wolves in more than 12,000 years, built with 20 edits across 14 genes. In May 2026, chicks hatched from a fully artificial egg, an early step toward the moa and the dodo. Yet, the real magic sits underneath.
To bring back a species, Colossal had to build a single, end-to-end system that can read a genome, use AI to model a desired change, write that change with multiplex editing, grow the organism and scale the process. Each of those steps used to be a separate discipline, in a separate lab, on a separate timeline. Colossal brought them into one workflow and demonstrated it in public, again and again.
WHAT THIS CAPABILITY COULD MAKE POSSIBLE
When you can design biology, the list of problems that become solvable gets very long, very fast. A few examples of what this platform could unlock:
Food: crops engineered to withstand drought and disease, feeding a hungrier, hotter world.
Health security: tools that track pathogens as they evolve, to help stop the next pandemic before it starts.
The environment: engineered enzymes that break down microplastics, wherever they are.
Biodiversity: reproductive technologies that could help pull endangered species back from the brink.
We call these living products: biology designed, built and scaled with the discipline of engineering. My favorite side effect is harder to measure. Somewhere right now, a 10-year-old is watching a dire wolf howl on YouTube and deciding to become a geneticist.
This is what abundance looks like when it’s written in DNA.
WHY NEOGENESIS
A capability like this doesn’t stay inside one company. Colossal has already spun out Form Bio (software for scientists), Breaking (microbes that digest plastic), Astromech (a biology model that learns from 3.8 billion years of evolution), two more companies in stealth and a bunch more coming in longevity, fertility, agriculture and AI-native genetic design.
Each of these companies starts with something rare in biotech: tools that have already worked in public, and a team that has used them.
Yianni and I wanted to help accelerate this tech, so we created NeoGenesis Capital.
We made one deliberate choice: go deep on a single platform rather than spread small bets across the whole field. It’s the same instinct behind XPRIZE. Find the most audacious team on the planet and help it go faster.
“Find the most audacious team on the planet, then help them go faster.”
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU
If you read this newsletter, you know the pattern: a technology gets digitized, looks deceptively slow for years, and then goes exponential. Biology is entering that curve right now. Here’s what that means, depending on where you sit:
If you’re an entrepreneur: every industry that touches a living thing (food, materials, medicine, pets, beauty) is about to get a programmable layer. Ask what you’d build if biology behaved like software.
If you’re an executive: put synthetic biology on your five-year roadmap now, while the best partnerships are still easy to get.
If you’re a student: learn biology and AI together. The most valuable scientists of the next decade will speak both languages.
If you’re a parent: show your kids the dire wolf videos. Wonder is the gateway drug to science.
Yianni and I spent the past year building NeoGenesis quietly. Today we’re saying it out loud.
One last question for you: if you could write one new organism into existence, what would it be? Tell us in the comments. (Ben has a very long list.)
To a future of abundance,
Peter
Disclosure: We are co-founders of NeoGenesis Capital and have a financial interest in the firm. Peter is also an investor in Colossal Biosciences. Colossal and Ben Lamm hold no ownership or financial interest in NeoGenesis Capital. This post is not an offer to sell or a solicitation of an offer to buy any security; NeoGenesis Capital has already held its initial closing and is not soliciting any investors publicly. Any offering by a fund management by NeoGenesis Capital is made only to eligible investors through definitive offering documents.

items.subject: Have We Seen the Last of the Cambrian Explosion in Quantum Computing Companies?
items.body:
View this post on the web at https://quantumzeitgeist.substack.com/p/have-we-seen-the-last-of-the-cambrian

Roughly half a billion years ago, in what counts as a short spell in geological time, life in the oceans went from soft, simple organisms to a seabed crowded with shells, legs, eyes and predators, and almost every major animal body plan we know today turns up in the rocks from that period, which is why palaeontologists call it the Cambrian explosion. Many of those early designs died out, but once the survivors claimed the available ways of making a living, nothing fundamentally new ever came along again, and I think quantum computing has just gone through its own version of that story...

items.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.a16z.news/p/wallet-wars

To hear more from Terry (Chief Strategy Officer at VGS), watch the companion a16z Show podcast here [ https://substack.com/redirect/fc8cc523-da81-40c5-a591-8e3faa2ea7b1?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ].
We’re also excited to announce Securing America’s Infrastructure Foundation today. SAIF is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, built to deliver AI and cybersecurity tools, hands-on support, and training to public institutions across America that otherwise lack access to AI tools. View it’s full mission here [ https://substack.com/redirect/0bc32329-dd35-46df-bfc0-5aeb5047c858?j=eyJ1IjoiNnpzZW5iIn0.r79EK39DqTrvjfrA7q3Ls0Ai90rVRXJ6fLgGtSMJWN4 ].
Agents such as Instinct, OAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse are bringing personal assistants into text messages and familiar apps. The promise is no longer just better answers; it is getting things done. If my agent can organize my kids’ soccer schedule, it can also order their cleats. If it can plan a trip, it can book the hotel. An assistant that understands my life becomes the starting point for much of my spending.
But completing those tasks requires something intelligence alone cannot provide: permission to pay. If your agent doesn’t have your credit card number, any recommendation from an agent becomes a “to do” list for me. With payment credentials in hand, the agent can complete the task for me.
So, of course, there is a scramble underway for what products and companies are going to help agents pay: enter the Wallet Wars.
Below the waterline, as wallets get connected to agents, there are two battles going on: one is over who can help my agent pay, and the other (more consequential one) is over who lets it transact as me. These seem like the same question but they are not! And the difference between the two is important, both for the user experience of “personal payment flows” (think loyalty programs) and for the economics of payments.
This is not a new challenge
In the early years of the internet, people were skeptical that anyone would ever buy something online. Giving your card number to a website seemed risky and unfamiliar. But online shopping was enough of a draw that people learned to trust the process. If history is a guide, just like last time, people will have no problem trusting agents to make payments on their behalf.
Part of what makes an online payment seem scary is that, to the user, the 16 digit card number represents both the identity of the paying account and the authority to initiate a payment. In reality, we’ve worked for decades on the underlying mechanics to make payments easy, safe, and secure, by effectively separating these two concerns. In the industry we call this “payment tokenization”.
Whenever you trust someone to save your card information (whether it be a merchant, a service, a wallet, or something else), they often also create a payment token. In addition to making the whole process more reliable and trustworthy, they also do nice things like, when your card expires, your Netflix subscription doesn’t have to pause - the actors behind the scenes coordinate, “you’re probably still you”, and keep your shows going. Payment tokenization is the site of many “inside-industry” power struggles for how you pay, that the user never sees - and I won’t inflict those stories on you, but payments professionals are very used to these kinds of standoffs.
Now we have these things called agents, which are a further evolutionary step in separating “the identity of the person / the account that’s going to pay” from “the authority to initiate a payment.” And, while it presents some new and interesting challenges which we’ll go through here, we’re not starting from zero - we’re building on years of precedent of how internet payments already work.
The war to connect
The fastest way to give an agent spending power is to connect a wallet that already holds the consumer’s credentials. Stripe’s Link (300M users), Shopify’s Shop Pay (250M users) and PayPal (400+M users) bring existing payment relationships to that contest, rather than asking consumers and merchants to start over.
For agent developers, the questions are straightforward: How many of my users already have a payment method stored with you? How many of the merchants support this wallet? Stripe and Shopify have moved quickly, powering payments for Muse and Instinct. But speed of integration is only one advantage. PayPal brings an established network of consumers and businesses. Perhaps agents can give PayPal a second act because the winning wallet needs not the prettiest checkout.
The war for reach
Because no wallet’s checkout button is accepted everywhere, wallets offer alternative paths to reach merchants. For example, Link gives an agent a single-use virtual card to make purchases on behalf of the customer.  In this flow, a merchant does not need to integrate Link; instead the agent can present its own virtual card during checkout.
While this expands its merchant acceptance, it doesn’t make the purchase equivalent to using the original card. Instead, two transactions are occurring. One between me and Stripe Link (using my card in the wallet) and one between Stripe Link and the merchant.
This can lead to some sub-optimal experiences. For example, imagine your agent buys something from Walmart. Walmart sees an opportunity to strengthen their customer relationship, and tells you: “We’d love to sign you up for Walmart+!” But if you try to accept their offer, what happens? The whole experience breaks, because the credit cards don’t match.
Stripe is building the AOL of agentic commerce
AOL packaged a messy online world into a curated experience; rather than read the news on an unknown website, AOL fetched the news and brought it to you, inside AOL.
For agentic payments, Stripe is building a similar walled garden where transactions occurring inside Stripe’s ecosystem never need to exchange credentials. If your agent shops at a Stripe merchant, Stripe can already charge the card on file without an agent touching it.
When transacting at non-Stripe merchants, Link has been the most aggressive wallet to use its own virtual cards for payment. This means that Stripe is actually buying the item on-your-behalf, rather than the agent acting as you. The good news is that the transaction succeeds. The bad news is the relationship between you and the merchant has changed and this creates problems outside the AOL-like walls.
Suppose I tell my agent to use my Chase Mileageplus card to book a flight at United. If my Link wallet charges that Mileageplus account, but pays United with a Stripe issued virtual card, the money may move without delivering everything I intended (where are my promised miles?). Link’s own terms warn that underlying card offers, benefits and rewards do not carry through in certain separate-payment-method transactions.
Stripe can reproduce the payment without necessarily preserving the relationship. That is the distinction between payment interoperability and relationship interoperability.
The war for routing
Now imagine my agent can access Link, Shop Pay and PayPal, with several cards available across them.
Which should it use?
I might prefer my airline card for airfare, another card for groceries, or the payment method already saved with a particular merchant. I may prioritize rewards for one purchase and purchase protection for another.
As we use agents going forward, “buy it” is not a complete payment instruction. The agent needs to understand my preferences, the merchant relationship and the consequences of each payment route. And when those interests conflict, whose economics should it optimize, the consumer’s, the merchant’s or the agent platform’s?
We are headed to a world where an agent needs a payment policy, not just a payment credential.
The war for liability
With so many intermediaries between me and my purchase, who bears liability for mistakes

Hi there,

Hope you're settling in well!

Scrape is the foundation of Firecrawl. One API call, any URL, and you get back clean markdown, structured JSON, screenshots, or whatever format your workflow needs.

A few things it handles:

* Clean LLM-ready markdown with no HTML noise
* Structured JSON from a schema or a prompt
* Batch scrape across multiple URLs in one request
* Full-page screenshots
* Smart caching, up to 5x faster on repeat requests

JavaScript rendering, proxies, rate limits, and anti-bot protections are handled behind the scenes.

Here are the sharpest conversations dominating tech and finance on X right now (as of Oct 15, 2026). The unifying theme is a violent repricing of the AI trade after a hotter-than-expected September CPI print collided with rising concerns about leverage and capacity.

1. Hot CPI + AI Infrastructure Selloff (CoreWeave as the Canary)
What happened: September CPI came in at 3.7% YoY (above ~3.6% expected), with core at 0.3% MoM. This pushed October Fed hike odds from the low-20s into the 40-50% range and sent the 10-year yield toward/above 5.3%. High-duration AI and chip names got hit hard: CoreWeave (CRWV) plunged ~15-16%, Asia chips (SK Hynix -10%+, Samsung, SoftBank) tanked, and broader tech followed. Nikkei and KOSPI saw sharp drops. Elon Musk replied “yikes” to a chart of CoreWeave’s bonds.

items.subject: 30 Side Hustle Prompts to Get Rich That Nobody Shares
items.body:
View this post on the web at https://aiengineeringinsider.substack.com/p/30-side-hustle-prompts-to-get-rich

Search “AI side hustle prompts” and you get the same list every time: “Give me 10 ways to make money with ChatGPT.” The model returns blogs, templates and social media management for local shops. Millions of people get that same list, so it is worth almost nothing.
We took a different approach. We read the research on how AI actually affects productivity and income. We read what founders, pricing experts, and regulators say about building a small business. Then we wrote 30 prompts that follow one rule: you bring the evidence, the model does the judging.
That is the part people rarely share. It is less exciting than a list of ideas, and it is much more useful.
First, what the research says
Here are five numbers we kept coming back to.
$885 vs. $200. Bankrate’s June 2025 poll of 2,616 US adults found side hustlers earn $885 a month on average, but the median is only $200. A small group earns far more than everyone else.
40% faster, 18% better. In a study published in Science (Noy and Zhang, 2023), 453 professionals finished writing tasks about 40% faster with ChatGPT, and evaluators rated the work 18% higher.
25% faster, 40% higher quality. In the Harvard Business School and BCG study of 758 consultants (Dell’Acqua et al., 2023), GPT-4 users finished 12% more tasks, 25% faster, with about 40% higher quality on tasks inside the model’s ability.
19 points worse. On a task outside the model’s ability, the same consultants were 19 percentage points less likely to get the right answer. The researchers call this the “jagged frontier.”
Earnings down 5.2%. After ChatGPT launched, writing freelancers on Upwork saw monthly jobs fall 2% and earnings fall 5.2% (Hui, Reshef and Zhou).
Put together, the lesson is clear. Generic AI output is now cheap, so selling it is a race to the bottom. AI is strong when it sorts, counts and critiques real data that you can check. It is risky when you trust it blindly.
So “rich” from a side hustle does not come from a prompt. It comes from three numbers that grow together:
Price: what one customer pays.
Volume: how many customers pay.
Retention: how much of the profit you keep and invest.
Every prompt below moves one of those numbers. Many ask for your income target so the model can work toward a real goal.
How to use these prompts
Each prompt follows the structure that the Anthropic and OpenAI prompting guides recommend: a role, your real data wrapped in tags like <reviews>One clear task, constraints, and an output format.
Three rules:
Evidence in, judgment out. Do not ask the model for facts you can collect yourself. Give it the facts and ask it to sort, score, and challenge them.
Verify anything that costs money. Prices, tax rules, and platform policies change. Confirm with the official source.
Keep your voice. Edit every draft before a customer sees it.
Replace everything in [BRACKETS]. After any answer, add this follow-up: “Which of your answers depend on assumptions I did not give you? List them.” That one line turns a confident answer into a checkable one.
The prompts are grouped into six stages: Find, Validate, Price, Build, Sell, Scale.
